(p-202) Surah al-Nahl is Meccan, and it has one hundred and twenty-eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

They used to hasten what they were promised of the Hour's coming and the descent of punishment upon them on the Day of Badr, mocking and denying the promise. So it was said to them: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, meaning: it is as if it has already come and occurred, although it is still awaited, because its occurrence is near. ﴿So do not seek to hasten it. Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ He, may He be exalted and glorified, is free of having any partner and of their associating others with Him. Here "mā" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah). The connection of this with their hastening is that their hastening was mockery and denial, and that is a form of shirk.

﴿He sends down the angels﴾. Read with *al-tahfif* (lightening, meaning without doubling the letter *zay*): Makki and Abu 'Amr.

﴿with the Spirit﴾: with the revelation or with the Qur'an, because each of them stands in the religion in the position the spirit holds in the body, or because each gives life to hearts that are dead through ignorance.

﴿by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, that: Warn﴾. Here *an* is *mufassira* (explanatory, introducing the sense of speech), because the sending down of the angels with the revelation carries the meaning of saying.

The meaning of *andhirū* (warn) is: know that the matter is that. It is from *nadhartu bi-kadha*, meaning "I informed him of such-and-such," when you inform him of it. The meaning is: inform the people of my saying, ﴿there is no god but I, so fear Me﴾, "*fa-ttaqūni*" meaning "*fakhāfūni*" (fear Me).

And with the *yā'* (reading *fa-ttaqūnī* with the final *yā'* as the first-person pronoun): Ya'qub.

Then he indicated His oneness and that there is no god but Him, by what He mentioned of things that no one other than Him can do: the creation of the heavens and the earth. This is His saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth; exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾. And [the verb] with the ta' (تَ, i.e., "takhalaqa"/"tu-shriku" forms) in both places is [read] by Hamza and ʿAli.

and the creation of man and what comes from him, which is His saying: ﴿He created man from a drop of semen; then behold, he becomes a open adversary﴾. That is: then behold, he is one who speaks clearly, disputing on his own behalf, contending with his adversaries, and making his argument clear, after having been a drop of semen with no sensation or movement. Or: then behold, he is an adversary to his Lord, denying his Creator, saying "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" And this is a description of man with shamelessness and persistence in ungratefulness for the blessing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 5:

It is the creation of what is necessary for them from the creation of livestock, for eating, for riding, for carrying their loads, and for all their other needs. This is his saying ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾. "Al-an'am" (the cattle) refers to the eight pairs, and it is most often applied to camels. Its grammatical status (i'rab) is as an object of a hidden verb that is explained by the apparent one, like His saying ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations﴾ [Ya-Sin: 39]. Or it is in coordination (ʿatf) with "al-insan" (man), meaning: He created man and the cattle, then said "He created them for you," that is, He did not create them except for you, O humankind.

﴿Therein is warmth﴾: "dif'" (warmth) is the name of what one is warmed by, of clothing made from wool, or fur, or hair.

﴿And benefits﴾: these are their offspring and their milk.

﴿And from them you eat﴾: he placed the adverbial phrase ("minha," from them) first, and this indicates restriction (ikhtisas). Yet eating from other than them is also permitted, because eating from them is the principal basis on which people rely for their livelihoods. As for eating from other than them, such as chickens, ducks, and game of land and sea, it is like what is not considered significant, and it falls within the category of enjoyment (tafakkuh) and luxury.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 6:

﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back [to the fold] in the evening and when you send them out to pasture in the morning.﴾ "Bringing them back" (tarihuna) means driving them from their grazing grounds (mara'i) back to their pens (maraḥ) in the evening. "Sending them out" (tasrahuna) means releasing them in the morning to their pasturing places (masarih).

God Most High bestowed favour by the beauty they add, just as He bestowed favour by the benefit derived from them, because beauty is among the concerns of the owners of livestock. When the herdsmen bring them back in the evening and send them out in the morning, the courtyards (afniyah) are adorned by their returning and their going out, their owners rejoice, and they gain for them esteem and honour in the eyes of people. The return (ijra'ah, al-iraha) is mentioned before the sending out (tasrih) because the beauty is more evident in the return, when they come back with full bellies and udders swollen with milk.

Qur'anic quotations are kept with the ﴿ ﴾ markers; the rest is translated as it stands.

﴿And it carries your burdens﴾ (aḥmālakum, your loads) ﴿to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves﴾. Reading shiqq (the first letter with a kasra) rather than shaqq: Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the shīn. Both are dialectal variants (lughatān) with the same meaning, hardship (al-mashaqqah). It has also been said that the one with a fatha is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of shaqqa al-amr ʿalayhi shaqqan (the matter was hard upon him), and its root meaning returns to shaqq (the cleft, the splitting), whereas shiqq (with a kasra) means half, as if half of one's strength departs because of the exertion one endures. The meaning is: it carries your loads to a land you could not reach even if camels had been created only with toil and hardship, let alone carrying your loads on your backs. Or its meaning is: you could not reach that land by them except with great hardship to yourselves. It has also been said that "your loads" (athqālakum) means your bodies, and from this comes "the two weights" (al-thaqalān) for the jinn and mankind, and from this comes ﴿And the earth will bring forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2], meaning the children of Adam. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾, in that He has shown mercy to you by creating these beasts of burden and facilitating these benefits.

The horses, mules and donkeys (He created) so that you may ride them and as an adornment. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "the livestock" (al-anʿām), meaning: He created these for riding and for adornment. Abū Ḥanīfa (may Allah have mercy on him) argued from this for the prohibition of eating horse meat, because He gave the reason for their creation as riding and adornment, and did not mention eating after mentioning it in the case of the livestock. The benefit of eating is stronger. The verse is brought to explain a blessing, and it is not fitting for the All-Wise to mention, in a context of favour, the lesser of two blessings and leave out the greater of them.

The accusative of "zīnatan" (adornment) is as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), coordinated with the position of "li-tarkabūhā" (so that you may ride them).

And He creates what you do not know of the kinds of His creatures, which is His saying: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾. From this kind of description He is exalted above having anything associated with Him.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 9:**

﴿And upon Allah is the direct way, and among them is one that deviates.﴾ The intended meaning of "the direct way" is the category as a whole, which is why He said, ﴿and among them is one that deviates.﴾ The word *qaṣd* is a verbal noun used in the sense of an active participle, meaning *qāṣid*. One says "a *sabīl qaṣd*" and "a *sabīl qāṣid*," meaning straight (p-205), as if it aims at the course that the traveler intends and does not turn away from. Its meaning is that guidance to the path that leads to the truth is incumbent upon Him, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl 92:12]. This is not an obligation, since nothing is obligatory upon Allah. Rather, He does this as a favor (*tafḍīl*). It was also said that the meaning is "and to Allah [the direct way belongs]." Al-Zajjaj said its meaning is: upon Allah is the clarification of the clear, straight path and the calling to it by means of proofs. "And among them is one that deviates" means: among the ways is one that inclines away from uprightness. ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all.﴾ He intended the guidance of *lutf* (divine grace, i.e., guidance through facilitation and bounty) by way of *tawfīq* (divine enablement) and favor, beyond the general guidance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 10:

﴿He it is who sends down water from the sky; from it you have drink﴾. "Lakum" (for you) is connected either to "anzala" (sent down), or it is the predicate of "sharab" (drink), which is what is drunk. ﴿And from it there is vegetation﴾, meaning the trees and plants on which the livestock graze, ﴿in which you pasture [your herds]﴾. From "sāmat al-māshiyah", when the livestock grazes, so it is "sā'imah" (pasturing), and its owner "asāmahā" (causes it to pasture). It derives from "al-sūmah", which is the mark (sign), because it leaves marks on the ground through the pasture.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 11:

﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and from every kind of fruit.﴾ He did not say "every kind of fruit" (kulla al-thamarat) because all of them exist only in Paradise; rather, He brought forth from each kind on the earth as a reminder. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾, so that they may draw evidence from it for Him and for His power and wisdom. The sign is like a clear proof.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 12:

﴿And He has subjected for you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; and the stars are subjected by His command.﴾ Read with the accusative for all of them, on the basis of: "and" [He made] "the stars subjugated [ones]" (musakhkharatin). "And the stars are subjugated [ones]" (musakhkharatun) only: Hafs. "And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjugated [ones]": Shami, on the basis of the inchoative (mubtada') and the predicate (khabar). ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason.﴾ He used the plural of "sign" (ayah) and mentioned reason ('aql), because the heavenly phenomena are more evident as proof of the overwhelming power, and clearer as testimony to majesty and greatness.

Translation of the passage:

﴿And what He has multiplied for you on the earth﴾ is in apposition (ma'tuf) to "the night and the day," meaning: what He has created in it of animals, trees, fruits, and other things. ﴿Of varying colors﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who take heed﴾ meaning: who take admonition.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 14:

﴿And He it is who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾ It is the fish (samak), and He described it as fresh (ṭarāwa), because spoilage hastens to it, so it is eaten quickly while fresh, out of fear of its spoiling. And [the reason] one does not break an oath by eating it, if one swears not to eat meat, is that the basis of oaths is custom (ʿurf). And whoever says to his servant, "Buy meat with these dirhams," and he brings fish, would deserve to be rebuked.

﴿and that you may extract from it ornaments (ḥilya) that you wear﴾ These are the pearl (lu'lu'a) and coral (marjān). ﴿that you wear﴾: what is meant by their wearing is the wearing of their women, but the women adorn themselves with them only for the sake of the men, so they are as if they were the men's adornment and clothing.

﴿And you see the ships plowing through (mawākhir)﴾ Ships running, moving swiftly, and cutting through the water with their prows. The word makhr means the cutting of water by the prow. ﴿in it﴾: in the sea. ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾: this is a conjunction with an omitted element, meaning: "that you may take heed, and that you may seek." The seeking of bounty is trade. ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ to God for what He has bestowed upon you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 15:

﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ — mountains that are fixed firmly — ﴿lest it should sway with you﴾ — out of dislike that it should lean with you or be agitated, or "lest it should sway with you." However, the omission of the governed term (al-mudaf, i.e., "lest it should sway with you" being "for fear of") is more common (lakinna hadhf al-mudaf akthar). It is said: when God created the earth, it began to sway, so the angels said: "No one can settle upon its back." Then it became steady, having been anchored with the mountains, and the angels did not know what it had been created from. ﴿And rivers﴾ — and He placed in it rivers, because "cast" (alqa) in it carries the meaning of "placed" (ja'ala). ﴿And roads﴾ — paths ﴿that you may be guided﴾ — to your destinations, or to the oneness of your Lord.

﴿And landmarks﴾: these are the markers of the roads, and everything by which the traveler (al-sabilah) is guided, such as a mountain and other things. ﴿And by the star they guide themselves﴾: the meaning of "the star" is the genus (al-jins), or it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Guards (al-Farqadan), the Daughters of the Bier (Banat Na'sh), and the Pole Star (al-Jadi). If you say: "And by the star they guide themselves" is departing from the usual pattern of discourse, in that "the star" is placed first and "they" (hum) is inserted, as if it were said: "And by the star, especially these people, especially they are guided," then who is meant by "they"? I say: it seems he intended the Quraysh, for they have guidance by the stars in their journeys, and they have a knowledge of this that was not the same for others. Thus gratitude was more obligatory upon them and reflection more binding on them, so they were singled out.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 17:

﴿Is He then who creates﴾ i.e., Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿like one who creates not﴾ i.e., the idols. The relative pronoun "man" (who), which is used for rational beings (ulu al-ʿilm, "possessors of knowledge"), is employed here because of their assumption, since they named them "gods" (ālihah) and worshipped them, so they treated them as though they were rational beings. Or, the meaning is: he who creates is not like one who creates not among the possessors of knowledge, so how much less so is that which has no knowledge. The reason it was not said "Is he who creates not like he who creates?" even though the context apparently requires it, is that this form constitutes a rebuke to those who worshipped idols and named them gods, likening them to Allah. For when they made something other than Allah like Allah in being named by His name and in being worshipped, they made Allah of the same kind as the created things and similar to them. So He rejected this from them with His words ﴿Is He then who creates like one who creates not?﴾ And this is a proof against the Mu'tazilah regarding the creation of acts. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is, so that you might recognize the corruption of what you are upon.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 18:

﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it.﴾ You would not be able to determine its number, and your capacity would not reach it, let alone your being able to fulfil the duty of thanking Him for it by rendering gratitude as it is due. He followed that with what He enumerated of His favours only as a reminder that what lies beyond them cannot be confined or counted. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ He overlooks your shortfall in rendering thanks for the favour, and does not cut it off from you because of your negligence. (p-208)

﷿ "And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose" — of your sayings and your deeds. And this is a warning (wa'id).

Wait, I need to correct that: I added an honorific symbol not in the source, and I should translate faithfully. Here is the faithful translation:

"And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose" [of your sayings and your deeds]. And it is a warning (wa'id).

﴿Those whom they call upon﴾, meaning the gods that the disbelievers call upon, ﴿besides Allah﴾. Reading it with the *ta'* (تَدْعُونَ, "you call upon") is the reading of all the readers except ʿĀṣim. ﴿They create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾

﴿Amwātun﴾ (they are dead), meaning: they are dead, ﴿not living﴾, and ﴿they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾. He negated from them the attributes of divinity by negating that they create and that they are living beings who do not die, and that they know the time of resurrection, and He affirmed for them the attributes of created things: that they are created, dead, and ignorant of the resurrection. The meaning of "dead, not living" is that if they were gods in reality, they would be living and not dead; that is, death is not permissible for them, whereas their situation is the reverse of this. The pronoun in "yub'athūn" (they are raised) refers to those who are invoked, meaning: they do not perceive when their worshippers will be raised. In this there is mockery of the polytheists, and [an indication] that their gods do not know the time of their being raised, so how could there be for them a time of recompense for their deeds from them for their worship? And in this there is evidence that resurrection is necessarily going to occur.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 22:

﴿Your God is one God.﴾ That is: it has been established by what has passed that divinity belongs to none other than Allah, and that your object of worship is one. ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are deniers﴾ of the Oneness, ﴿and they are arrogant﴾ toward it and toward acknowledging it.

﴿Lā jaram﴾ (indeed, truly) ﴿anna Allāha yaʿlamu mā yusirrūna wa mā yuʿlinūn﴾ — that is, their secret and their open (deeds), so He will recompense them; and this is a warning. ﴿Innahu lā yuḥibbu al-mustakbirīn﴾ — from tawhid, meaning the polytheists.

"And when it is said to them" — to these disbelievers — "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients." (ماذا) is in the accusative, governed by (أنزل), meaning: "What thing has your Lord sent down?" Or it is in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), meaning: "What is it that your Lord has sent down?" Then (أساطير) is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject. It is said that this is the statement of the al-Muqtasimun (the "dividers"), those who divided up the entrances of Makkah, turning people away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the delegations of pilgrims asked them about what had been sent down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they would say: "Tales of the ancients," that is, the stories and falsehoods of the ancients, the singular of which is (ustura). But when they saw the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informing the people of his truthfulness and that he is a Prophet, they were the ones who said (khayran), "good."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 25:

﴿That they may bear their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge.﴾ Meaning: they said that to mislead the people, so they bear the burdens of their misguidance in full, and part of the burdens of those who went astray through their misguidance, which is the burden of misguiding, because the one who misleads and the one who is led astray are partners. The lam here is for causation (lam al-ta'lil). ﴿Without knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: they mislead those who do not know that they are misguided. ﴿Surely evil is what they bear﴾: the place (mahall) of "ma" is in the nominative (raf').

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 26:

﴿Indeed, those before them plotted, but Allah came at their structure from its foundations﴾. That is, from the direction of its foundations, which are the pillars. This is a parable, meaning that they set up structures with which to plot against the messengers of Allah, so Allah made their destruction come through those very structures, like the case of a people who built a edifice and propped it up with pillars, then the edifice was attacked through its pillars, such that they were shattered, and the roof fell down upon them, and they died and perished. The majority of scholars hold that what is meant by this is Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built the tower (al-sarh) in Babylon, whose height was five thousand cubits, and it was said: two farsakhs. So Allah sent the wind, and it collapsed upon him and his people, and they perished. Thus "Allah came" means His command to uproot them. ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾, that is, from where they did not expect and did not anticipate.

Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them (يُخْزِيهِمْ), that is, humiliate them with the torment of disgrace, in addition to what they were punished with in the world. ﴿And He will say: Where are My partners?﴾ (شُرَكائِيَ), with the attribution to Himself, as a relating of their attribution [of partners to Him], in order to rebuke them with it in a mocking manner toward them. ﴿Those whom you used to oppose concerning them﴾, that is, whom you used to be hostile to and dispute with the believers about their affair. Nafi' read "تُشاقُّونِي" (tushāqqūnī), meaning "you used to oppose Me concerning them," because opposing the believers is as if it were opposing God.

﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾, that is, the prophets and the scholars of their communities who used to call them to faith and admonish them, but they did not heed them and opposed them; they say this out of gloating over them. Or they are the angels. ﴿Indeed, disgrace today﴾, the exposure (الفَضِيحَةَ), ﴿and evil﴾, the punishment (العَذابَ), ﴿are upon the disbelievers.﴾

﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾: Hamza reads it with the letter *yāʾ* (بِالياءِ), as *yatawaffāhumu*, and likewise what follows it. ﴿While they are wronging themselves﴾ by disbelieving in God. ﴿Then they will offer submission﴾: that is, reconciliation and surrender, meaning they submitted and came to the opposite of what they had been in the world, of opposition (*shiqāq*). They said, ﴿We did not do any evil,﴾ and they denied what had been found in them of disbelief and enmity. So the people of knowledge (*ulū al-ʿilm*) refuted them and said, ﴿Yes, indeed God is Knower of what you used to do,﴾ so He will recompense you for it. This too is a form of gloating (*shamātah*). And likewise.
﴿So enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. Wretched is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ Jahannam (Hell).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 30:

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful (of shirk)﴾ "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good." The reason why this (word) is in the accusative (naṣb) and "Asāṭīr" (fables) is in the nominative (rafʿ) is that the implied sense here is "He sent down good," so they matched the answer to the question; whereas the implied sense there is "It is fables of the ancients," so they deviated in the answer from the question. ﴿For those who did good in this world﴾, i.e., they believed and did righteous deeds, or they said "There is no god but Allah," ﴿is good﴾, in the nominative (bi-l-rafʿ), i.e., reward, security and gain. It is a substitute (badal, grammatical apposition) for "good" in the statement of those who were mindful, i.e., they said this statement, so he placed before it the naming of it as "good" and then related it. Or it is a resumed statement (kalām mustaʾnaf), a promise to the speakers, and he made their saying part of their good deeds. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾, i.e., for them in the Hereafter is what is better than it (this world), like His saying: "So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the goodly reward of the Hereafter." ﴿And how excellent is the abode of the mindful﴾, the abode of the Hereafter. The object of praise is omitted because it was mentioned earlier.

﴿Gardens of perpetual abode﴾ (جَنّاتُ عَدْنٍ) is a khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtada' (subject), or it is mukhassas bil-madh (specified for praise). ﴿They will enter them﴾ (يَدْخُلُونَها) is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier). ﴿Rivers flow beneath them, and for them therein is whatever they wish. Thus Allah rewards the righteous.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 32:

﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾ — pure, clean of wronging their own souls through disbelief, since this is set in contrast to those who wrong themselves. ﴿They will say, "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾ It has been said: when the believing servant is about to die, an angel comes to him and says, "Peace be upon you, O friend of Allah. Allah sends you His greetings of peace and gives you the glad tidings of Paradise." And it is said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿Enter the Garden for what you used to do﴾ — that is, for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 33:

﴿Are they waiting﴾ — what are these disbelievers waiting for? ﴿except that the angels should come to them﴾ to seize their souls. With the ya' (they, third person), ʿAlī and Ḥamzah read it as ﴿yaʾtiyahum﴾ [in the sense of "should come to them"]. ﴿Or that the command of your Lord should come﴾ — i.e., the all-destroying punishment, or the Resurrection. ﴿Thus﴾ — like that same action of polytheism and denial — ﴿did those before them do﴾, ﴿and Allah did not wrong them﴾ by destroying them, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they did what made them deserving of destruction.

﴿So the evils of what they had done befell them﴾: the recompense for the evils of their deeds. ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾: and the recompense for their mockery encompassed them. (p-٢١٢)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 35:

﴿And those who associated partners (with Allah) say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without Him."﴾ This is a statement that came from them in mockery, and if they had said it out of genuine belief, it would have been correct. ﴿Nor would we have prohibited anything without Him﴾ means the baḥīrah (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the sā'ibah (a camel released to graze freely), and similar things. ﴿Thus did those before them do﴾ means: they denied the messengers, prohibited what was lawful, and said the same as what they said, in mockery. ﴿So is it upon the messengers except the clear conveyance?﴾ Except that they convey the truth and make clear the falsehood and ugliness of polytheism.

We sent a messenger to every community, [saying]: "Worship Allah" — by which he meant: "Single Him out [in worship]" — "and shun the Taghut" (al-Taghut: Satan, meaning obedience to him), "Some of them Allah guided" — because of their choosing guidance — "and upon some of them misguidance was necessarily due," i.e., it clung to them because of their choosing it. "So travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers," where Allah destroyed them and emptied their dwellings of them.

Then He mentioned the obstinacy of Quraysh and the eagerness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for their faith, and informed him that they belong to the category of those upon whom misguidance is decreed. So He said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray.﴾ [Read as] "yahdi" with a fatha on the ya and a kasra on the dal by al-Kufi (ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, the Kufan reciters); the rest read it with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the dal. The reasoning for the latter is that "man yudillu" (whom He leads astray) is the subject (mubtada') and "la yahdi" (He does not guide) is its predicate (khabar). ﴿And they have no helpers﴾, who would prevent them from the operation of Allah's decree upon them, or ward off from them His punishment which He has prepared for them.

And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ is coordinated (*ma'tūf*, conjoined) with ﴿And those who associated partners with Allah said﴾ [al-Nahl 16:35].

﴿Allah will not resurrect one who dies.﴾ "Balā" (بلى, "yes, indeed") is an affirmation of what follows a negation, meaning: rather, He will resurrect them. ﴿A promise binding upon Him, a truth﴾: "waʿdan" (وَعْدًا, "a promise") is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) emphasizing what "balā" indicates, because "yabʿathu" (يَبْعَثُ, "He resurrects") is a promise from Allah. He clarified that fulfilling this promise is true. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that His promise is true, or that they will be resurrected.

"So that He may make clear to them" is connected to what is indicated by "Bala" (Yes, indeed), meaning: He will resurrect them so that He may make clear to them. The pronoun refers to those who die, and it includes both believers and disbelievers. "That about which they differ" is the truth. "And that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars" in their saying that Allah does not resurrect whoever dies.

Verse 40: "Indeed, Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, 'Be,' and it is." That is: then it comes to be. With the accusative (fa-yakūna, read as naṣb), it is read by Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī) and ʿAlī, in response to "kun" (be). "Qawlunā" is the subject (mubtada'), "an naqūla" is its predicate (khabar), and "kun fa-yakūnu" comes from kāna al-tāmma (complete kāna), meaning coming into being and existence. That is: when We intend the existence of a thing, there is nothing except that We say to it, "Come into being," and it comes into being without any delay. This is an expression of the swiftness of bringing into existence. It shows that His will cannot be resisted, and that its existence at the moment of His will is not delayed, like the existence of the one commanded at the command of an obeyed commander, when the obedient, compliant subject responds without any speaking there. The meaning: the bringing into existence of every thing within God's power is with this ease, so how could the resurrection, which is among the things within His power, be beyond Him?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 41:

﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah﴾ — for His right and for His countenance — ﴿after they had been wronged﴾. They are the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions. The people of Makkah wronged them, so they fled with their religion to Allah. Among them were those who emigrated to Abyssinia (al-Habasha) and then to Madinah, so he combined the two migrations (hijratayn); and among them were those who emigrated directly to Madinah. ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾ — ḥasanah is an attribute of the verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning a good settlement (tabwi'ah ḥasanah); or it means ﴿We will surely settle them in a good abode (mubā'ah ḥasanah)﴾, which is Madinah, where its people gave them shelter and supported them. ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾ — the pause here is obligatory (lāzim), because the response (jawāb) of ﴿if they only knew﴾ is omitted. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning: if they knew that, they would have been eager for the religion; or it refers to the emigrants, meaning: if they knew it, they would have increased in their striving and their patience. (p-214)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 42:

﴿Those who were patient﴾. That is: they are the ones who were patient, or I mean: those who were patient. Both are a form of praise. That is: they were patient in leaving the homeland, which is the sanctuary of Allah, beloved in every heart, so how much more so in the hearts of a people for whom it is the place where their heads were first laid (their birthplace). And [they were patient] in striving (mujahadah) and in giving up their lives in the way of Allah. ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾. That is: they entrust their affair to their Lord and are content with what has befallen them in the religion of Allah.

When Quraysh said, "God is too exalted for His messenger to be a human being," there was revealed: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed⦆ — "nuhi" (We reveal) is read by Hafs as "nūḥī" [with the first letter vowelled as nūn], [the revelation being conveyed] through the tongues of the angels. ﴿So ask the people of the reminder﴾ — the People of the Book — ﴿that they may inform you⦆ that God did not send to the earlier nations except human beings. It is also said: the "reminder" refers to the Book, because it is an admonition and a warning to the heedless. ﴿if you do not know﴾.

ﷻ"With the clear proofs and the Scriptures." That is: with the miracles and the books. The preposition "bi" (with) is linked either to "rijālan" (men), as a qualifier of it, meaning men associated with the clear proofs; or to "arsalnā" (We sent) understood, as though it were said: "With what were the messengers sent?" and the answer is "with the clear proofs"; or to "nūḥī" (We reveal), meaning: We reveal to them with the clear proofs; or to "lā ta'lamūn" (you do not know).

His statement ﴿So ask the people of the reminder﴾ [al-Naḥl: 43] is an interjection (i'tirāḍ) against the aforementioned interpretations.

His statement ﴿And We have sent down to you the reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿so that you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them﴾, in the reminder, of what they were commanded to do, what they were forbidden from, what they were promised, and what they were threatened with, ﴿and that they may reflect﴾ upon its reminders, ﴿so that they may take heed﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 45:

﴿Are those who devised evil schemes then secure﴾ — i.e., the evil schemes (al-makarat al-sayyi'at). They are the people of Makkah, and what they schemed against was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿that Allah might cause the earth to swallow them up﴾, as He did with those who came before them, ﴿or that the punishment might come upon them from where they do not perceive﴾ — i.e., suddenly (baghtah). (p-215)

Translation:

﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾, moving about in their travels and their trading journeys, ﴿so they cannot escape﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 47:

﴿Or He seizes them while they are in a state of apprehension.﴾

[They are] in a state of fear (mutakhawwifin), which is that He destroys a people before them, so they become apprehensive, and then the punishment seizes them while they are fearful and anticipating [it]. This is the opposite of His saying: ﴿from where they do not perceive﴾. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾, in that He forbears with you and does not hasten [the punishment] against you despite your deserving it. The meaning is: when He does not seize you despite what is among you, it is only His tenderness that protects you and His mercy that shields you.

**"Have they not seen"** is also read with the *tā'* (تَرَوْا, "have they not seen" as a second-person-inflected form) by Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Abū Bakr. **"to what Allah has created"**: *mā* (مَا, "what," a relative pronoun, *mawṣūlah*) is connected to *khalaqa Allāh* (خَلَقَ اللهُ, "Allah has created"), and its explanation is left unspecified (*mubham*). **"of a thing whose shadows incline"**: *yatafayya'u ẓilāluhu* (يَتَفَيَّأُ ظِلالُهُ) means that they return from one place to another. The reading with *tā'* (يَتَفَيَّأُ, "its shadows are inclined") is that of Baṣrī. **"from the right and the left"**: *al-yamīn* (الْيَمِينِ) means *al-aymān* (the right sides), and *al-shamā'il* (الشَّمَائِلِ) is the plural of *shimāl* (left). **"prostrating to Allah"**: *sujjadan* (سُجَّدًا) is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) referring to *al-ẓilāl* (the shadows). On the authority of Mujāhid: when the sun declines, everything prostrates. **"and they are humbled"**: *dākhirūn* (دَاخِرُونَ) means *ṣāghirūn* (humbled, abased). It is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun in *ẓilālihi* (ظِلالِهِ), because it carries the sense of a plural. It is pluralized with the *wāw* and *nūn* ending because *al-duxūr* (abasement) is a characteristic of rational beings. Alternatively, because among all that Allah has created, from everything that has a shadow, there are some who are rational, so the masculine rational plural was given precedence.

The meaning is: "Have they not seen what Allah has created of bodies that have shadows, whose shadows incline from their right and left sides?" That is, the shadows return from one side to the other, submitting to Allah, the Exalted, not resisting Him in what He has subjected them to of inclining. The bodies themselves are also abased and humbled, submitting to the acts of Allah upon them, not resisting.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 49:

﴿And to Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures (dābba)﴾ "Min" (from) is an explanation (bayān) of "mā" (whatever) in "what is in the heavens and what is on the earth" together, on the basis that in the heavens there are creatures that crawl (yadibbūna) within them as the humans (al-anāsīy) crawl on the earth; or it is an explanation of "what is on the earth" alone. What is meant by "what is in the heavens" is their angels, and by His saying ﴿and the angels﴾ are meant the angels of the earth, from among the guardians (al-ḥafaẓa) and others. It has been said: what is meant by the prostration of the accountable ones (al-mukallafīn) is their obedience (ṭā'a) and worship ('ibāda), and by the prostration of others is their submission (inqiyād) to the will of Allah. The meaning of submission encompasses both, so they do not differ; therefore it is permissible to express both by a single word. ﴿Mā﴾ was used because it is suitable for rational beings and others; had ﴿man﴾ been used, it would have encompassed only rational beings, ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 50:

﴿They fear their Lord﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿they do not wax proud﴾, meaning: they do not wax proud, being fearful. ﴿Above them﴾: if you attach it to ﴿they fear﴾, its meaning is that they fear Him lest He send down upon them a punishment from above them; and if you attach it to ﴿their Lord﴾ as a circumstantial clause from Him, its meaning is that they fear their Lord as the One who dominates them, the Subduer, like His saying ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18]. ﴿And they do what they are commanded﴾. In this there is evidence that the angels are responsible (mukallafun), governed by the command and the prohibition, and that they are between fear and hope.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 51:

﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods. He is only one God.﴾ If you ask: They combine the number and the numbered beyond "one" and "two," saying "ʿindī rijālun thalāthah" (I have three men), because the numbered noun is devoid of indication of the specific number; but "rajul" and "rajulān" (a man and two men) are numbered nouns that contain an indication of the number, so there is no need to say "rajulun wāḥid" (one man) and "rajulān ithnān" (two men, two)? I say: the noun that carries the meaning of singularity and duality indicates two things: the class (jinsiyyah) and the specific number. When it is intended to show that what is meant by it is the number, it is accompanied by something that emphasizes it, and thereby it indicates the intention toward it and the concern with it. Do you not see that if you said "innamā huwa ilāhun" (He is only a god) and did not emphasize it with "wāḥid," it would not be good, and it would seem that you were affirming divinity, not oneness? ﴿So fear Me, and only Me.﴾ The speech shifts from the third person (ghaybah) to the first person (takallum), and this is from the method of iltifāt (shift of address), and it is more eloquent in encouraging fear than his saying "fa-iyyāhu fārhabū" (so fear Him), "fārhabūnī" (fear Me). Ya'qub (Ya‘qūb) [reading].

"And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is the religion" (ay al-ṭāʿah, meaning obedience). ﴿wāṣiban﴾ means obligatory and established, because every blessing comes from Him, so obedience to Him is obligatory for every person upon whom a blessing has been bestowed. It is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) in which the adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf) functions as the governing element, "عَمِلَ فِيهِ (p-٢١٧) الظَرْفُ". Or, "and to Him is the reward always," meaning the reward and the punishment. ﴿Will you then fear other than Allah?﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 53:

﴿And whatever blessing you have, it is from Allah﴾. Whatever blessing has reached you of well-being, wealth, and abundance, ﴿it is from Allah﴾; it is from Allah. ﴿Then, when harm touches you﴾, namely sickness, poverty, and drought, ﴿to Him you cry out for help﴾; you do not humble yourselves in supplication except to Him. Al-judar (crying out for help) is raising the voice in supplication and seeking aid.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 54:

﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord.﴾ The address in "And whatever blessing you have is from Allah" (wa ma bikum min ni'matin): if it is general (ʿamm), then the intended meaning of "a group" (farīq) is the disbelievers (al-kafara). If the address is to the polytheists (mushrikun), then His saying "of you" (minkum) is for explanation (li-l-bayan), not for partitioning (li-l-tab'idh), as if He said: "then behold, a disbelieving group, and they are you." It is also permissible that among them there are those who take heed, as in His saying: ﴿So when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate (muqtasid)﴾ [Luqman: 32].

Translation:

﴿That they may deny what We have given them.﴾ [They act] as though they had made their aim in associating partners [with God] the denial of the blessing, [namely] the removal of harm from them. Then He threatened them, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves; you will soon know.﴾ This is a shift to direct address, as a warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 56:

﴿And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided them﴾. That is, to their gods. The meaning of "what they do not know" is that they call them gods and believe about them that they harm, benefit, and intercede with Allah, whereas that is not so, because they are inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit. Or, the pronoun in "what they do not know" refers to the gods, meaning: to things not described with knowledge and not perceiving. Did they assign a share for them in their livestock and their crops or not? They used to assign that to them as a means of drawing near to them. ﴿By Allah, you will surely be questioned﴾ is a warning, ﴿about what you used to fabricate﴾, namely that they are gods and that they are deserving of being drawn near to. (p-218)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 57:

﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾ Khuza'ah and Kinanah used to say that the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ a declaration that He is exalted above having offspring attributed to Him, or an expression of wonder at their saying. ﴿And for themselves what they desire﴾ meaning sons. The word "ma" may be in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada') with "for them" (lahum) as its predicate (khabar), or in the accusative, as a conjunction (ataf) upon "daughters". The phrase "Glory be to Him" is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. That is: they attributed to themselves what they desire of males.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 58:

﴿When one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ That is, "ṣāra" (became), so that "ẓalla" (he remained/became), "amsā" (he became in the evening), "aṣbaḥa" (he became in the morning), and "bāta" (he spent the night) are used with the meaning of "ṣayrūra" (becoming), because most births take place at night, so that his day remains troubled, his face darkened from grief and from shame before people. ﴿And he is suppressed with rage﴾, that is, filled with anger toward the woman.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 59:

﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of that whereof he has been given tidings﴾ He hides himself from them because of the badness of what he has been given tidings of, and because of their reproach (ta'yir). He talks to himself and reflects. ﴿Shall he keep it despite disgrace?﴾ Shall he keep what he has been given tidings of, in humiliation and abasement? ﴿Or bury it in the dust?﴾ Or bury it alive (ya'idu, i.e., wa'd, infanticide). ﴿Surely evil is what they judge﴾ in that they attribute to God the child whose status with them is this, and assign to themselves what is the opposite of this description.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 60:

﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description﴾ The "evil description" (ṣifat al-sawʾ) is the need for male offspring, the dislike of females, and burying them alive out of fear of poverty. ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ which is self-sufficiency above all the worlds and freedom from the attributes of created beings. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾ the Overpowering in carrying out what He wills, ﴿the Wise﴾ in granting respite to His servants.

﴿And if God were to take the people to task for their wrongdoing﴾ – for their disbelief and their sins – ﴿He would not leave upon it﴾ – upon the earth – ﴿any creature﴾ at all, ﴿and He would destroy them all because of the evil of the wrongdoers.﴾ On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (p-219) – may God be pleased with him – "The houbara bustard dies in its nest because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." On the authority of Ibn Mas'ud – may God be pleased with him – "The dung beetle nearly perished in its hole because of the sin of the son of Adam." On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas – may God be pleased with them both – "from a creature – from a polytheist – that crawls." ﴿But He delays them until an appointed term﴾, that is, the term of each individual, or a time required by wisdom, or the Resurrection. ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾

**Verse 62:** ﴿And they attribute to God what they dislike.﴾ That is, what they dislike for themselves: daughters, partners in their leadership, and contempt for their messengers. And they attribute to Him the basest of their wealth, while they give their idols the most honourable of it. ﴿And their tongues describe the lie﴾ despite that; that is, they say the lie. ﴿That for them is the good (al-husna) with God﴾, which is Paradise, if resurrection is true, like His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely with Him there is the good (al-husna) for me﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. "That for them is the good" is a substitute (badal) for "the lie."

﴿Without doubt, for them is the Fire, and they will be left behind (mufrathun).﴾ "Mufrithun" (with kasra and no tashdid) is read by Nafi', and "mufarritun" (with tashdid) by Abu Ja'far. The one with fatha means: brought forward to the Fire and hastened toward it, from afrattu fulanan and farratahu in seeking water, when you send him ahead; or: forgotten and abandoned, from afrattu fulanan khalfi, when you leave him behind and forget him. The one with kasra and without tashdid is from al-ifrat (excess) in sins, and the one with tashdid is from al-tafrit (neglect) in acts of obedience, i.e., falling short in them.
