Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 66:

﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾. As for the reading with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* (*nuqsīhim*, "We give you to drink"), it is transmitted by Nāfi', al-Shāmī and Abū Bakr. Al-Zajjāj said: "*saqaytuhu*" and "*asqaytuhu*" have the same meaning. Sībawayh mentioned that *al-an'ām* ("livestock") is among the singular nouns that occur on the pattern of plurals (*asmā' mufradah al-wāridah 'alā af'āl*), and for this reason the pronoun referring to it is singular. As for ﴿in their bellies﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 21] in Surat al-Mu'minīn, it is because its meaning is plural. The clause here is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nāf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as if it were said: "What is the lesson?" So He said: ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾ ﴿from between dung and blood, pure milk﴾. That is, God creates the milk as an intermediary between the dung and the blood, which surround it, while between it and them is a barrier (*barzakh*) so that neither of them transgresses upon it in colour, taste or smell; rather it is pure of all of that. It is said: when the beast eats fodder and it settles in its paunch (*karish*), the paunch cooks it, so its lowest part becomes dung, its middle part milk, and its uppermost part blood. The liver is set over these three kinds, dividing them: it sends the blood through the veins and the milk into the udders, while the dung remains in the paunch and then passes out. In that there is a lesson for whoever reflects.

Shaqīq was asked about sincerity (*ikhlāṣ*), and he said: it is the separation of the deed from its defects, like the separation of milk from between dung and blood. ﴿Palatable to the drinkers﴾: easy to pass down the throat. It is said that no one has ever choked on milk.

The first *min* (in ﴿min bayni farthin wa-damin﴾) is partitive (*li-l-tab'īḍ*, indicating a part of a whole), because milk is a part of what is in their bellies. The second *min* indicates the starting point of a limit (*ibtidā' al-ghāyah*).

(p-٢٢١)

**Verse 67:** ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, you take from them an intoxicant and a good provision. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason.﴾

67 – The phrase ﴿وَمِن ثَمَراتِ النَخِيلِ والأعْنابِ﴾ is connected to an omitted verb whose implied sense is "and We give you to drink" (وَنُسْقِيكم), meaning: "from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes," that is, from their juice (عَصِيرِهِما). The verb is omitted because "nuskīkum" (We give you to drink) mentioned before it indicates it. The words ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنهُ سَكَرًا﴾ are an explanation and a clarification of the nature of the drink. Alternatively, ﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ﴾ may be read with ﴿ومِنهُ﴾ as a repetition of the prepositional phrase "from" (min) for emphasis. The pronoun in ﴿مِنهُ﴾ refers to the omitted genitive construction, which is "juice" (al-'aṣīr).

"Sakar" (سَكَرًا) means intoxicant, meaning wine (al-khamr). It is named by the verbal noun of "sakira" (سَكِرَ), with the forms "sakaran" and "sukran," like "rashida rashadan" and "rushdan." There are then two views. The first is that this verse precedes the prohibition of wine, and so it is abrogated (mansūkhah). The second is that it combines reproach and favor.

It has also been said that "sakar" means nabīdh (نَبِيذ), which is the juice of grapes, raisins, or dates that is boiled until two-thirds of it evaporates, then left until it ferments. This is permitted according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on them both, up to the point of intoxication. They argue from this verse, from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Wine is forbidden in itself, and intoxication comes from every drink," and from many reports.

﴿وَرِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾ means vinegar (al-khall), grape syrup (al-rubb), dates, raisins, and other things besides these. ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ means: "Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 68:

﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee﴾ that ﴿take for yourselves houses in the mountains﴾. Here "an" (that) is the explanatory "an" (an-mufassira), because inspiration (al-iyha') carries the meaning of speech (al-qawl). Al-Zajjaj said: The singular of al-nahl (bees) is nahlah, like nakhl (palm trees) and nakhlah (a palm tree), and the feminine form (in the verb) is in consideration of this. And "min" in ﴿min al-jibal﴾ (from the mountains) ﴿and from the trees and from what they erect﴾ (p-222) — they raise from the roofs of the house or what they build for the bees — in the mountains, the trees, and the houses, from the places in which they make honey. "Min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), because they do not build their houses in every mountain, every tree, and everything that is erected. The pronoun in "ya'rishun" (they erect) refers to the people; and with the ra' vowelled with a damma, it is read by Ibn 'Amir (Shami) and Abu Bakr.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 16, verse 69:**

﴿Then eat of all the fruits﴾, i.e., build the houses, then eat every fruit you desire. When you have eaten it, ﴿then follow the ways of your Lord﴾, i.e., enter the paths that I have inspired and taught you in the making of honey. Or, when you have eaten the fruits in distant places away from your houses, then return to your houses by following the ways of your Lord, without going astray in them. ﴿Docile﴾ is the plural of *dhalūl* (ذَلُولٍ), and it is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the ways (*subul*), because God Most High made them easy and smooth. Or it is a state of the pronoun in *fa-uslukī* (فاسْلُكِي), meaning: "and you are docile, submitting to what you have been commanded, not refusing." ﴿From their bellies there comes forth a drink﴾, meaning honey, because it is something drunk, which they expel from their mouths. ﴿Its colors vary﴾: some of it is white, yellow and red, according to youth, middle age and old age, or according to the colors of their food. ﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾, because it is among the beneficial medicines. Hardly any electuary (*ma'jūn*) among the electuaries is mentioned by physicians without honey in it. The purpose is not that it is a cure for every patient, just as every medicine is not like that. Its being indefinite (*tankīruh*, تَنْكِيرُهُ) serves to magnify the healing that is in it, or because in it there is some healing, since an indefinite noun in an affirmative sentence is restrictive (*takhuṣṣu*).

A man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about the diarrhea (*istiṭlāq baṭn*) of his brother, and he (ﷺ) said: "Give him honey to drink." The man came back and said: "It has only made it worse." He (ﷺ) said: "God has spoken the truth, and the belly of your brother has lied. Give him honey to drink." He gave him honey to drink, and he was cured.

It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him): "Honey is a healing for every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts. So hold fast to the two healings: the Qur'an and honey."

Among the innovations (*bida'*) of the Rawafid (a term for the Shi'a), it is claimed that the intended meaning of "the bee" (*naḥl*) is 'Ali and his people. It is reported from some of them that a man said in the presence of al-Mahdi: "The bee is only the Banu Hashim; knowledge comes forth from their bellies." A man said to him: "May God make your food and drink from what comes forth from their bellies." Al-Mahdi laughed and related this to al-Mansur, and they made it a jest among their jokes.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾ on the wondrous nature of its affair (p-223), so that they know that God deposited in it knowledge of this, and gave it intelligence, just as He gave people of understanding their minds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 70:

﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die﴾ by seizing your souls from your bodies. ﴿And among you is one who is brought back to the most abject age﴾ to its most degraded and lowest state, which is seventy-five years, or eighty, or ninety. ﴿So that he does not know, after having knowledge, anything﴾ so that he forgets what he knew, or so that he does not come to know any increase in knowledge beyond his knowledge. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing﴾ of the ruling of transformation to the abject from the perfect, or to annihilation from life. ﴿Competent﴾ over changing whatever He wills, as He wills, among things.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 71:

﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision.﴾ That is, He made you differ in provision, so He gave you more excellent provision than what He gave your slaves, though they are humans like you. ﴿So those who have been favoured⦆ in provision, meaning the owners, ﴿will not give up their provision to⦆ those ﴿whom their right hands possess,⦆ so that they would be equal with them. It was fitting that you return the surplus of what you have been given to them, so that you would be equal in clothing and food. ﴿So they are equal in it.⦆ This is a nominal sentence occurring in the place of a verbal sentence, in the accusative position, because it is the answer to the negation with the fa' (fa, "so"). Its implied form is: "So those who have been favoured will not give up their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they would be equal with their slaves in provision." This is a parable that Allah struck for those who set up partners for Him. He said to them: "You do not make yourselves equal with your slaves in what I have bestowed upon you, nor do you make them partners in it, and you do not accept that for yourselves. So how did you accept that you make My slaves partners with Me?" ﴿Then do they deny the favour of Allah?⦆ Read with the ta' (tā') by Abu Bakr, and he made that part of denying the favour.

﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾, i.e., of your own kind. ﴿And has made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren (ḥafadah)﴾. Ḥafadah is the plural of ḥafid (one who hastens in obedience and service), i.e., one who hurries in obedience and service. From this is the saying of the one who is devoutly obedient (qānit) in the supplication: "And to You we hasten and serve." It is disputed regarding it. It is said: they are the in-laws through the daughters. It is also said: they are the children of children. The meaning is: "And He has made for you ḥafadah," i.e., servants who serve in your interests and help you. (p-٢٢٤) ﴿And has provided you with good things﴾, i.e., some of them, because all good things are in Paradise, and the good things of this world are a sample of them. ﴿Will they then believe in falsehood?﴾ This is what they believe about the benefit of the idols and their intercession. ﴿And in the blessing of Allah﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 67], i.e., Islam, ﴿they disbelieve﴾. Or, the falsehood is Satan, and the blessing is Muhammad (ﷺ). Or, the falsehood is what Satan embellishes for them of prohibiting the baḥīrah (a she-camel whose ear was slit and set free), the sā'ibah (a camel set free to roam), and others, and the blessing of Allah is what He has made lawful for them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 73:

﴿And they worship besides Allah that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens and the earth, [any] at all﴾. That is, the idol (ṣanam), and it is an inanimate object (jamād) that cannot possess the power to provide anything. So al-rizq (provision) may be used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) and may also mean that which is provided. If you intend the verbal noun, you put shay'an (anything) in the accusative governed by it, meaning: it cannot possess the power to provide anything. If you intend the provided thing, then shay'an is a substitute (badal) for it, meaning "a little." And "from the heavens and the earth" is a complement (ṣilah) of al-rizq if it is a verbal noun, meaning: it does not provide rain from the heavens nor vegetation from the earth; and it is a qualifier (ṣifah) if it is a noun for that which is provided. The pronoun in ﴿and they are not able﴾ refers to mā, because it carries the sense of the gods after he said "does not possess," [i.e., it refers to the gods] according to the wording (lafẓ) [being singular], and the meaning is: they do not possess provision, nor is it possible for them to possess it, nor is that attainable from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 74:

﴿So do not strike forth comparisons for God﴾. "Do not make for God a likeness, for He has no like," i.e., "do not make for Him partners." "God knows" that He has no like among creation, "while you do not know" that. Or it means: God knows how to strike comparisons, while you do not know that. The first interpretation is the preferred one.

Then He set forth a parable, saying: ﴿Allah sets forth a parable: a slave, owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with goodly provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly﴾. "A slave" is a substitute (badal) for "a parable" (mathalan). "Secretly and openly" are two verbal nouns (masdarani) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: your parable, in your associating idols with Allah, is the parable of one who equates a slave owned and incapable of disposing of anything with a free owner whom Allah has provided with wealth, so that he disposes of it and spends from it (p-225) as he wills. The slave is qualified as "owned" to distinguish him from the free man, since the term "slave" (ʿabd) applies to both of them, as both are servants of Allah. And "who has no power over anything" is to distinguish him from the mukatab (one contracting to purchase his freedom) and the ma'dhun (one licensed to trade), for these two have power to dispose of things. The "man" (man) may be a qualifying noun, meaning: and a free man whom We have provided, so that it corresponds to "a slave"; or it may be a relative pronoun.

﴿Are they equal?﴾ He used the plural pronoun to indicate plurality, meaning: the two groups are not equal. ﴿Praise be to Allah; but most of them do not know﴾ that praise and worship belong to Allah.

Then He added further clarification, saying: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything﴾. Al-abkam (the mute) is one who was born dumb, so he neither understands nor makes himself understood. ﴿And he is a burden upon his master﴾, i.e., a weight and a dependant upon whoever is in charge of his affairs and supports him. ﴿Wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾, meaning: wherever he sends him or dispatches him to fulfil some need or to take care of an important matter, he is of no benefit and brings no success. ﴿Is he equal to one who commands justice﴾, i.e., one who is sound in his senses, beneficial, capable and possessed of good judgement and piety, so that he commands people to justice and goodness. ﴿And he﴾ in himself ﴿is upon a straight path﴾, upon a righteous conduct and an upright religion. This is a second parable which He coined for Himself, and for the effects of His mercy and blessing that He pours out upon His servants, and for the idols, which are dead and neither harm nor benefit.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 77:

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: the knowledge of what is hidden in them from the servants, and whose knowledge is concealed from them, is exclusive to Him. Or he intends by the unseen of the heavens and the earth the Day of Resurrection, on the basis that its knowledge is hidden from the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, and none of them has been informed of it. ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but like the blink of an eye﴾ in its nearness of occurrence and swiftness of establishment, ﴿or it is nearer﴾ — ﴿or it is nearer﴾ meaning the matter is nearer. This is not due to any doubt on the part of the one addressed; rather the meaning is: be in its occurrence according to this consideration. It has also been said: "Rather, it is nearer." ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾; so He is capable (p-226) of establishing the Hour and resurrecting the creation, since that is among the things within His power.

Then He indicated His power by what follows, saying: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers﴾. Ali [al-Kisa'i] read ﴿ʾummahātikum﴾ with a kasra on the alif and a fatha on the mim, matching the kasra of the nun [in minna-style harmony, i.e., ʾimmahātikum], while Hamza read it with a kasra on both. The ha' is an augmentation in ʾummahāt for emphasis, just as it was added in ʾarāqa, so that it became ʾahrāqa; its addition in the singular is anomalous. ﴿You knew nothing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while you were not knowing anything [of the right of the Benefactor who created you in the wombs]. ﴿And He made for you hearing, sight, and hearts, that you might give thanks﴾. That is: He assembled these faculties in you only as instruments for removing the ignorance into which you were born, and for acquiring knowledge and acting upon it, by giving thanks to the Benefactor, worshipping Him, and discharging His rights. The word al-afʾidah (hearts) is the plural of fuʾād, like al-aghribah for ghurāb; it is one of the plurals of paucity (jumūʿ al-qillah) which have taken the place of plurals of abundance (jumūʿ al-kathrah), because no other usage of it has been heard.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 79:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ (with the ta' read by Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami) and Hamzah) ﴿the birds subjected﴾ made subservient ﴿for flight in the air of heaven﴾, being made subservient for flying by means of the wings and the causes that enable them to do so, ﴿in the atmosphere of the sky﴾, which is the air distant from the earth in the direction of height, ﴿none holds them up﴾ in their grasping, their spreading out and their hovering ﴿except Allah﴾ by His power. In this there is a negation of what imagination depicts concerning the inherent property of the natural powers. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾

(This is) because creation has no independence from the Creator.

﴿And Allah has made for you from your houses a place of rest.﴾ It is *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ul*, meaning that which one finds rest in and turns to for refuge, whether a house or a beloved companion. ﴿And He has made for you from the skins of livestock houses,﴾ which are domes of soft leather (*adam*), ﴿that you find light to carry in the striking of camp, the pitching and the moving,﴾ ﴿on the day of your departure,﴾ read with a sukun on the *'ayn* by the Kufans and the Syrians, and with a fatha on the *'ayn* by the others. *Dha'n* (the *'ayn* with fatha or sukun) means departing on a journey. ﴿and on the day of your settling,﴾ meaning your residence in your dwellings. The meaning is that they are light for you in the times of both travel and residence, on the basis that "day" here means "time." ﴿And from their wool﴾ i.e., the wool of sheep, ﴿and their fur﴾ and the fur of camels, ﴿and their hair﴾ and the hair of goats, ﴿furnishings﴾ household goods, ﴿and provision﴾ and things from which benefit is derived, ﴿for a time﴾ a period of time.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 81:

﴿And God has made for you, of what He has created, shades;﴾ like the trees and the roofs. ﴿And He has made for you, among the mountains, places of shelter;﴾ the plural of kinn (shelter), which is that which conceals you of a cave or a grotto. ﴿And He has made for you garments;﴾ these are shirts and clothes made of wool, flax and cotton. ﴿which protect you from the heat;﴾ and they also protect from the cold, but He suffices with mention of one of the two opposites, and because protection from the heat is more important to them, since cold is slight and bearable. ﴿And garments that protect you from your violence;﴾ and coats of mail of iron which turn away from you the weapons of your enemy in your fighting. Ba's (violence, might) is the intensity of war, and sirbal (garment) is a general term that applies to whatever is made of iron or other than it. ﴿Thus He completes His favour upon you, that you may submit;﴾ i.e., that you may reflect upon His overflowing favour, so that you believe in Him and submit to Him.

﴿But if they turn away﴾ — they turn away from Islam — ﴿then your duty is only the clear conveyance﴾; that is: there is no blame upon you in this, for what is incumbent upon you is the manifest delivering (of the message), and you have done it.

They know the favour of Allah, which We have enumerated, through their statements, for they say that it is from Allah. ﴿Then they deny it﴾ through their actions, when they worship other than the Benefactor, or (they deny it) in hardship and then in ease. ﴿And most of them are the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the deniers, those who do not acknowledge (it). Or, the favour of Allah is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ): they knew it, then they denied it out of obstinacy. ﴿And most of them are the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the rejecters who deny with their hearts. ﴿Then﴾ indicates that their denial is a matter of astonishment after the attainment of knowledge (p-228), because the due of one who recognizes a favour is to acknowledge it, not to deny it.

**[Commentary of al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on 16:84]**

﴿And [mention] the Day﴾ — its being in the accusative is governed by "remember" (udhkur). ﴿We shall raise up﴾ — i.e., gather. ﴿From every nation a witness﴾ — a prophet who will bear witness for them and against them, to their affirmation and denial, and to their faith and disbelief. ﴿Then no permission will be given to those who disbelieved﴾ — to offer an excuse. The meaning is: they have no argument, and the withholding of permission indicates that they have neither argument nor excuse. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ — nor will they be asked to seek contentment; that is, it will not be said to them, "Satisfy your Lord," because the Hereafter is not an abode of action. The meaning of "then" (thumma) is that they will be tested, after the testimony of the prophets, peace be upon them, with something more grievous and more overwhelming than that, namely that they will be prevented from speech, so permission will not be given to them to put forward an excuse or to present an argument.

﴿And when those who did wrong﴾ disbelieved ﴿see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them﴾, i.e., the punishment after entering (the Fire), ﴿nor will they be given respite﴾, meaning they will not be granted time before it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 86:

﴿And when those who associated partners [with God] see their partners﴾, their idols which they worshipped, ﴿they will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners"﴾, i.e., our gods which we made partners [with You], ﴿"those whom we used to call upon besides You"﴾, i.e., worship. ﴿But they will throw back at them the word: "Indeed, you are liars."﴾ i.e., they answered them with denial, because they were inanimate objects that did not know who worshipped them. It is also possible that they denied them in calling them partners and gods, glorifying God above association.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 87:

﴿And they will offer submission to Allah that Day﴾: meaning, those who did wrong. Ilqa' al-salam (offering submission) is "al-istislam" (surrender) to the command and judgment of Allah after refusal and arrogance in the world. ﴿And what they used to fabricate will be lost to them﴾: that is, it will vanish from them, namely their claim that Allah has partners, and that these partners would help them and intercede for them, when those (partners) denied them and disowned them.

(p-229)

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ in themselves, ﴿and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾, and drive others to disbelief, ﴿We shall add to their punishment, punishment upon punishment﴾, i.e., a punishment for their disbelief and a punishment for their barring [others] from the way of Allah. ﴿For what they used to corrupt﴾, by virtue of their being corrupters of people through barring [them].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 89:

﴿And on the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves﴾ — He means their Prophet, because he (ﷺ) used to raise up the prophets of the nations from among them, [each one] from among their own people. ﴿And We bring you, O Muhammad, as a witness against these﴾ — against your nation. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation﴾ — eloquent — ﴿of everything﴾ — of the matters of the religion. As for the explicitly stated rulings, it is evident; and likewise what is established by the Sunnah (the Prophetic traditions), or by consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars), or by the statement of the Companions, or by analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy), because the source of all of these is the Book, where it commands us to follow His Messenger (ﷺ) and obey him, in His saying: ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. And it urges us toward consensus in it by His saying: ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 115]. And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approved for his nation that they follow his Companions, by his saying: "My Companions are like the stars; whichever of them you follow, you will be guided." And they exerted independent reasoning, applied analogy, and laid down the paths of independent reasoning and analogy, although He commanded us to do so in His saying: ﴿So take warning, O you who have eyes﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. Thus the Sunnah, consensus, the statement of the Companion, and analogy are all grounded in the explanation of the Book; so we conclude that it was an explanation of everything. ﴿And a guidance and a mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ — a guide to the truth, a mercy for them, and good news to them of Paradise.

﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾, meaning equality in rights among you, abandoning injustice, and giving every person with a right his right. ﴿And good conduct﴾, meaning kindness toward one who has wronged you. Or they are the obligatory (al-farḍ) and the recommended (al-nadb), because the obligatory must inevitably involve some shortfall, which the recommended makes up for. ﴿And giving to kindred﴾, meaning giving to relatives, which is maintaining ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim). ﴿And He forbids immorality (al-faḥshā')﴾, meaning the sins that are extremely ugly in their repulsiveness, ﴿and wrongdoing (al-munkar)﴾, meaning what reason disapproves of, ﴿and transgression (al-baghy)﴾, meaning seeking to domineer through oppression and arrogance. ﴿He admonishes you﴾, a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a new independent sentence. ﴿That you may be reminded﴾, meaning that you may be admonished by the admonitions of Allah.

This verse was the cause of the conversion of Uthman ibn Maz'un. He said: "I had only embraced Islam out of shyness before him (peace be upon him), because of how often he presented Islam to me. Faith had not settled in my heart until this verse was revealed while I was with him, and then faith settled in my heart." I recited it to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and he said: "By Allah, it has a sweetness, and its outer surface has a beauty, its upper part bears fruit, and its lower part is abundant with water. It is not the words of a human being." Abu Jahl said: "Indeed, his god commands the noble qualities of character."

It is the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an concerning good and evil, and for this reason every preacher (khaṭīb) recites it from the pulpit at the end of every sermon, so that it may be a comprehensive admonition for everyone commanded and everyone forbidden.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 91:

﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have made a pledge﴾. It is the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) upon Islam. ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. ﴿And do not break oaths﴾, namely the oaths of the pledge of allegiance, ﴿after their confirmation﴾, after their being bound by the Name of Allah. Akkada (أكّد) and wakkada (وكّد) are two eloquent dialects (lughatan fasihatan), and the original root is the waw, with the hamzah being a substitute for it. ﴿And you have made Allah your guarantor (kafil)﴾, meaning a witness and an overseer, because the guarantor (kafil) watches over the condition of the one guaranteed and has authority over him. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows what you do﴾, of righteousness and of breaking [oaths], and He will recompense you for it.

This passage is from al-Nasafi's commentary (Madarik al-Tanzil) on 16:92.

﴿And do not be﴾ in breaking oaths ﴿like her who untwisted her thread after it had been strong﴾, like the woman who used to toil over her spinning after she had made it firm and tightly twisted, and then made it ﴿into pieces﴾. Ankath is the plural of nakth, which is that which is unravelled after being twisted. It is said that she was Rayta, a foolish woman who used to spin, she and her female slaves, from dawn until noon, and then she would order them and they would unravel what they had spun.

﴿Taking your oaths as a means of deceit﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) like "ankathan". Dakhalan is one of the two objects of tattakhidhu, meaning: do not break your oaths, taking them as a means of deceit (dakhal) ﴿among yourselves﴾, that is, as corruption and treachery.

﴿Because one community is greater than another﴾: because of [the fact that] there is a community, meaning the group of Quraysh, ﴿that is more numerous than another community﴾, that is, more numerous in count and richer in wealth than another community, the group of believers. Here "hiya arba" is a subject-predicate construction in the position of a raised (marfu') attribute of "ummatun", and "ummatun" is the subject of takun, which is complete (tammah), and it is not a separating pronoun (fasl) because it occurs between two indefinite nouns.

﴿Allah only tests you thereby﴾: the pronoun refers to the verbal noun (masdar), meaning: He tests you by their being more numerous, in order to see whether you hold fast to the cord of fidelity to the covenant of Allah and to the oaths of allegiance you swore to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or whether you are deceived by the multitude and wealth of Quraysh and the scarcity and poverty of the believers. ﴿And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ﴾, when He recompenses you for your deeds with reward and punishment. This contains a warning against opposing the religion of Islam.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 93:

﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made you one community﴾ (ummah wahidah), upright (hanifah) and submitting (muslimah). ﴿But He leads astray whom He wills﴾, meaning whoever He knows chooses misguidance. ﴿And guides whom He wills﴾, meaning whoever He knows chooses guidance. ﴿And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, and you will be recompensed for it.

﴿And do not take your oaths as a means of deceit among you﴾. He repeated the prohibition on taking oaths as a means of deceit among them, to emphasize it for them and to show its gravity. ﴿Lest a foot slip after it was firmly planted﴾: lest your feet slip from the path of Islam (al-Islam) after they were firmly established on it. The word "foot" (qadam) is made singular and indefinite to magnify the idea that a single foot slipping from the way of truth after it had been firmly on it is serious, so how much more so when many feet slip? ﴿And you would taste evil﴾ in this world ﴿for what you hindered﴾ by your turning away ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ and your departure from the religion, or by your hindering others. For if they broke the oaths of allegiance (bay'ah) and apostatized, they would make breaking them a precedent (sunnah) for others to follow. ﴿And for you there is a great punishment﴾ in the Hereafter.

"And do not sell [your oath] for a small price" — "and do not exchange (wa la tastabdilu) the covenant of Allah" and the pledge of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "for a small price," a trifling, passing gain of this world. It is said that some people from among those who had embraced Islam in Makkah, Satan adorned for them, because of their anxiety at what they saw of the dominance of Quraysh and their oppression of the Muslims, and since they had been promising them that if they returned from [Islam] they would break what they had pledged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah made them firm. ﴿What is with Allah﴾ of the reward of the Hereafter ﴿is better for you, if you knew﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 96:

﴿What is with you﴾ of the transient goods of this world ﴿will come to an end, but what is with Allah﴾ of the treasuries of His mercy ﴿is lasting﴾, not coming to an end. "And We will surely reward" — with the nun (نون) it is read by Makki and ʿAsim (ʿĀṣim). ﴿Those who were patient﴾ over the harm of the polytheists and the hardships of Islam ﴿–their reward We shall give them according to the best of what they used to do﴾.

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female﴾. "Man" (مَن) is indefinite and encompasses both sexes, but its apparent sense is for males. So He clarified it with His words "whether male or female," so that the promise would include both sexes. ﴿while being a believer﴾: He stipulated faith, because the deeds of disbelievers are not counted, and this indicates that deeds are not part of faith. ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾: that is, in this world. ﴿And We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾: Allah promised them the reward of this world and the Hereafter, like His words ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 148]. This is because the believer who does righteous deeds, whether wealthy or poor, lives a good life. If he is wealthy, this is obvious. If he is poor, he has with him what makes his life pleasant, which is contentment and acceptance of Allah the Exalted's decree. As for the wicked person, his situation is the reverse: if he is poor, it is obvious, and if he is wealthy, greed does not let him enjoy his life. It has been said: the good life is contentment, or the sweetness of obedience, or knowledge of Allah, sincerity of standing before Allah, sincerity in adhering to Allah's command, and turning away from all other than Allah. (p-233)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 98:

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ meaning: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, ﴿seek refuge in Allah﴾. Here he expressed the intention of the act with the wording of the act, because it is its cause (sabab). The fa' (fa, "then") indicates sequence (ta'qib), since the recitation that is preceded by seeking refuge is from the righteous deed mentioned. ﴿from Satan﴾, meaning Iblis, ﴿the accursed﴾, meaning the one cast out (al-matrud) or the cursed (al-mal'un).

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I recited in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and I said: A'udhu billahi as-Sami' al-'Alim min ash-shaytan ar-rajim (I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed). He said to me: Say: A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ar-rajim (I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed). Thus did Jibril, peace be upon him, recite it to me."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 99:

﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾ over Iblis, ﴿authority﴾ meaning domination and dominion, ﴿over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾. So the believer who relies upon Him does not accept his whisperings.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 100:

﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally (yatawallawnahu)﴾ They take him as a protector (waliyyan) and follow his whisperings (wasawisahu), ﴿and those who, because of him, are associates (in worship)﴾. The pronoun (al-damir) refers either to their Lord or to Satan, i.e., because of him.

And when We substitute one verse in place of another, (﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾). The substitution of one verse for another is the *naskh* (abrogation), and Allah, exalted is He, abrogates the sacred laws (*shara'i'*) with other laws for a wisdom that He sees. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿and Allah knows best what He sends down﴾. The reading with the lightened form (*bi-al-takhfif*, reading *baddalna* as *badalna*) is attributed to Makki and Abu 'Amr. ﴿They say, "You are only a fabricator"﴾ is the *jawab* (response clause) of *idha* (when). His words, "and Allah knows best what He sends down," are an *i'tiraD* (interjected parenthetical clause). They used to say that Muhammad (ﷺ) mocks his companions: he commands them today to do one thing and forbids them from it tomorrow, bringing them what is easier. They lied, for he abrogated the harder with the easier and the easier with the harder. ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾ the wisdom behind that. (p. 234)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 102:

﴿Say: The Holy Spirit (Rooh al-Qudus) has brought it down﴾ — meaning Jibril (peace be upon him). He is ascribed to al-Qudus, which is purity, just as one says "Hatim of generosity" (Hatim al-Jud). The intended meaning is "the Holy Spirit" (al-Ruh al-Muqaddas), and "Hatim al-Jawad" (Hatim the generous). Al-Muqaddas is the one purified from sins. ﴿from your Lord﴾ — from His presence and by His command. ﴿with truth﴾ — this is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: He sent it down connected with wisdom. ﴿so that He may strengthen those who believe﴾ — so that He may test them through abrogation (naskh), until, when they say about it, "It is the truth from our Lord and wisdom," because He is Wise and does only what is wisdom and correctness, it is ruled for them that they have firmness of foot, soundness of certainty, and tranquility of hearts. ﴿and as guidance and good tidings﴾ — two objects of purpose (maf'ul lahuma), coordinated with the position (mahall) of "li-yuthabbita"; the estimated sense is: as a strengthening for them, and guidance, and glad tidings. ﴿for the Muslims﴾ — and in this there is an implicit allusion (ta'rid) that the opposites of these qualities occur for others.

And We surely know that they say, "Only a human being teaches him." They meant by this a boy who belonged to Huwaytib, who had embraced Islam and whose Islam was sound. His name was ʿĀʾish or Yaʿīsh, and he was a possessor of books. Or it was Jabr, a Roman boy belonging to ʿĀmir ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. Or it was the two slaves Jabr and Yasār, who used to read the Torah and the Gospel, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to hear what they recited. Or it was Salmān al-Fārisī. ﴿The tongue of the one to whom they incline﴾, with the yāʾ and the ḥāʾ vowelled with fatha (yalḥadūna), is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī. ﴿is foreign, and this is clear Arabic tongue﴾. That is: the tongue of the man towards whom they incline their speech away from uprightness is a foreign tongue, not clear, while this Qur'an is a clear Arabic tongue, possessing clarity and eloquence. This is a refutation of their words and a nullification of their slander. This clause, namely "the tongue of the one to whom they incline is foreign," has no grammatical place (lā maḥall lahā, i.e., it has no i'rab, no syntactic position), because it is a resumed statement (mustaʾnafah) that serves as a reply to their saying. Lisān means language (lughah). It is said alḥada al-qabr and laḥadahu, and he is mulḥid and malḥūd, when he inclines its digging away from straightness, so that he digs in one side of it. Then the term was borrowed for every deviation from uprightness, so they say alḥada fulān fī qawlihi (someone deviated in his saying) and alḥada fī dīnihi (he deviated in his religion). From this comes the word mulḥid (heretic, one who deviates), because he inclines his doctrine away from all religions. (p. 235)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 104:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿Allah will not guide them﴾ as long as they choose disbelief, ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, for their disbelief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 105:

﴿Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies﴾ against Allah. That is: the fabrication of lies is only fitting for one who does not believe, because he does not expect any punishment for it. This is a rebuttal of their saying, "You are only a fabricator" (innama anta muftarin). ﴿And those﴾ is a reference to those who do not believe; that is: and those ﴿are the liars﴾ in the true sense, the perfect ones in lying, because denying the signs of Allah is the greatest of lies. Or: and those are the liars in their saying, "You are only a fabricator."

They allowed that ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief﴾ could be a conditional (*shart*, the conditional particle) functioning as a subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject), with its response (*jawab*) omitted, because the response of "whoever expands" (*man sharaha*) indicates it. It is as if it were said: "Whoever disbelieves in God, upon them is wrath." ﴿Except one who has been compelled while his heart is at rest with faith﴾, meaning settled in it. ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, that is, is content in himself with it and believes in it. ﴿Upon them is wrath from God, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

It could also be a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾ [al-Nahl: 105], with ﴿And those are the liars﴾ [al-Nahl: 105] made a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraD*) between the substitute and what it substitutes. The meaning is: only those who fabricate lies are those who disbelieve in God after their belief. He excepted from them the one who is compelled, so he does not fall under the ruling of fabrication. Then He said: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from God.﴾

It could also be a substitute for the subject, which is ﴿those﴾ (*ulaika*), meaning: "And whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, they are the liars." Or it could be a substitute for the predicate, which is ﴿the liars﴾, meaning: "And those are the ones who disbelieve in God after their belief." It could also be in the accusative (*nasb*) by way of censure (*dhamm*).

It has been narrated that some people from Makkah were tested, so they apostatized. Among them was one who was compelled, and he uttered the word of disbelief with his tongue while he held to faith. Among them was ʿAmmar. As for his parents, Yasir and Sumayya, they were killed, and they were the first two people killed in Islam. "It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), 'Indeed ʿAmmar has disbelieved.' He said: 'No! Indeed ʿAmmar is filled with faith from his hair to his feet,' and 'faith has mingled with his flesh and his blood.' Then ʿAmmar came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and said, 'What is with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said.'"

What Abu ʿAmmar did is more excellent, because in patience under killing there is strengthening (*i'zaz*) of Islam.

﴿That﴾ refers to the threat, which is the incurring of wrath and a great punishment. ﴿Because they preferred﴾ chose ﴿the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾, meaning: because of their preferring this world to the Hereafter. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ as long as they choose disbelief.

Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts, their hearing, and their sight. So they do not reflect, nor do they give ear to admonitions, nor do they see the path of right guidance. ﴿And those are the heedless﴾ — meaning, the complete ones in heedlessness, because heedlessness of reflecting upon the outcomes is the utmost degree of heedlessness and its final limit.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 109–110:

﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the ones who are the losers.﴾ ﴿Then indeed your Lord﴾ "Then" (thumma) indicates the great distance between the state of these and the state of those [before them]. ﴿for those who emigrated﴾ from Makkah. That is: it is for them, not against them; meaning, He is their Protector and Helper, not their enemy or one who forsakes them. It is like when sovereignty belongs to a man rather than being against him, so that he is protected, benefited, and not harmed. (p-237) ﴿after they were tried﴾ with punishment and compulsion to disbelief. "Futinu" (futinu) is the reading of Ibn Amir (Shami), meaning: after they had punished the believers, and then they embraced Islam. ﴿Then they struggled﴾ against the polytheists after the emigration ﴿and were patient﴾ in the struggle. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after these [deeds]﴾, i.e., after these actions, which are the emigration, the struggle and the patience, ﴿is All-Forgiving﴾ toward them for what came from them of uttering the word of disbelief out of taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation) ﴿Most Merciful﴾, who does not punish them for what they said under compulsion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 109–110:

﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the ones who are the losers.﴾ ﴿Then indeed your Lord﴾ "Then" (thumma) indicates the great distance between the state of these and the state of those [before them]. ﴿for those who emigrated﴾ from Makkah. That is: it is for them, not against them; meaning, He is their Protector and Helper, not their enemy or one who forsakes them. It is like when sovereignty belongs to a man rather than being against him, so that he is protected, benefited, and not harmed. (p-237) ﴿after they were tried﴾ with punishment and compulsion to disbelief. "Futinu" (futinu) is the reading of Ibn Amir (Shami), meaning: after they had punished the believers, and then they embraced Islam. ﴿Then they struggled﴾ against the polytheists after the emigration ﴿and were patient﴾ in the struggle. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after these [deeds]﴾, i.e., after these actions, which are the emigration, the struggle and the patience, ﴿is All-Forgiving﴾ toward them for what came from them of uttering the word of disbelief out of taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation) ﴿Most Merciful﴾, who does not punish them for what they said under compulsion.

ليس في النص ما يمنع الترجمة، وهذه ترجمته:

﴿يَوْمَ تَأْتِي﴾ منصوب بـ"رحيم" أو بـ"اذكر" ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ تُجادِلُ عَنْ نَفْسِها﴾. وإنما أُضيفت النفس إلى النفس، لأنه يُقال لعين الشيء وذاته: "نفسُه"، وفي نقيضه: "غيرُه"، والنفس: الجملة كما هي. فالنفس الأولى هي الجملة، والثانية عينها وذاتها. فكأنه قيل: يوم يأتي كل إنسان يجادل عن ذاته، لا يهمّه شأن غيره، كلٌّ يقول: نفسي نفسي. ومعنى المجادلة عنها الاعتذار، كقولهم: ﴿هَؤُلاءِ أضَلُّونا﴾ [الأعراف: ٣٨]، ﴿رَبَّنا إنّا أطَعْنا سادَتَنا وكُبَراءَنا﴾ [الأحزاب: ٦٧] الآية، ﴿واللهِ رَبِّنا ما كُنّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [الأنعام: ٢٣]. ﴿وَتُوَفّى كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ما عَمِلَتْ﴾ أي: تُعطى جزاء عملها وافيًا، ﴿وَهم لا يُظْلَمُونَ﴾ في ذلك.

﴿And Allah sets forth a parable﴾: that is, He made the town whose condition is this a parable for every people whom Allah blessed, but whom the blessing made insolent, so they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah sent down His vengeance upon them. It is permissible that it means a hypothetical town described with this attribute. It is also possible that among the towns of earlier peoples there was a town whose condition was this, and Allah made it a parable for Makkah, as a warning of the kind of end it might meet. ﴿It was secure﴾ from killing and captivity, ﴿at peace﴾, not disturbed by fear, because tranquility (al-ṭumaʾnīnah) accompanies security, while unease (al-inziʿāj) and anxiety (al-qalaq) accompany fear. ﴿Its provision came to it abundantly﴾, plentiful, ﴿from every place﴾, from every land, ﴿but its people denied﴾ ﴿the favours of Allah﴾. The word أنعم is the plural of نِعْمَةٍ (niʿmah) formed without counting the tā' marbūṭah, as in دِرْعٌ / أدْرُعٌ; or it is the plural of نُعْمٌ (nuʿm), as in بُؤْسٌ / أبْؤُسٌ. ﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾. The words "making taste" (al-idhāqah) and "garment" (al-libās) are both metaphors (isti'arah). The metaphorical "making taste" is applied to the metaphorical "garment". The reason this is correct is that "making taste" is, for them, used in the sense of its literal meaning, because it is common in afflictions and hardships and what touches people of them. They say: "So-and-so tasted misery and harm" and "He made him taste punishment". The perception of the effect of harm and pain is compared to the perception of the taste of bitterness and foulness. As for "garment", it is used as a comparison, because it envelops the wearer, for whatever covers a person and clings to him of certain calamities. As for applying "making taste" to the "garment of hunger and fear", it is because, since the phrase has come to refer to what covers and clings to a person from these two, it is as if it were said: "So He made them taste what covered them of hunger and fear."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 16, verse 113:

﴿And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿But they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾, that is, while they were in a state of being mixed up with wrongdoing. They said: it was the killing by the sword on the Day of Badr. It was narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to the people of Makkah, in the years of drought, food, and he distributed it among them. Then Allah said to them, after He had made them taste hunger:"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 114:

﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾ — upon the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ) — ﴿lawful and good﴾ — as a replacement for what you used to eat, which was unlawful and foul, from the wealth obtained through raids and usurpation and foul earnings. ﴿And be grateful for the blessing of Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾ — that is, obey Him — or, if your claim that you worship Allah by worshipping the gods is true, since they are your intercessors with Him.

Then He enumerated for them the things Allah has forbidden, and forbade them from forbidding and permitting according to their own desires, so He said: ﴿Indeed He has forbidden to you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ "Innama" (indeed... only) is for restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: the thing forbidden is this, and not the baḥīra and its kind. The rest of the verse has already been explained.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 116:**

﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe as falsehood﴾: the word **هو** (*huwa*, "it") is in the accusative (*manṣūb*) governed by **لا تقولوا** (*lā taqūlū*, "do not say"). That is, "do not say falsehood concerning what your tongues describe of the livestock as lawful and unlawful in your saying, ﴿This that is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-An'am: 139], without that description being based on revelation or on analogy (*qiyās*) derived from it." The **لام** (*lām*, "concerning") in it is like it in your saying, "Do not say concerning what God has made lawful that it is unlawful." The phrase **﴿هذا حلال وهذا حرام﴾** ("this is lawful and this is unlawful") is a substitute (*badal*) for "falsehood." You may also put **الكذب** (*al-kadhib*, "falsehood") in the accusative governed by **تصف** (*taṣif*, "describe"), make **ما** (*mā*) a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*), and attach **"هذا حلال وهذا حرام"** to **لا تقولوا**, so that the meaning is: "Do not say, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful,' and this is for the description your tongues give to falsehood," that is, "Do not forbid or make lawful on account of a saying that your tongues utter and that circulates in your mouths, not on account of proof and clear evidence, but as a bare statement and a claim without demonstration."

His saying **"تصف ألسنتكم الكذب"** ("your tongues describe falsehood") is from eloquent speech: he made their saying as though it were the very essence of falsehood. So when their tongues utter it, they have clothed falsehood in its finery and given it its form, as in your saying, "Her face describes beauty, and her eye describes enchantment."

The **لام** in **﴿لتفتروا على الله الكذب﴾** ("that you may fabricate falsehood against God") is a causal *lām* that does not carry the sense of purpose (*gharaḍ*). ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate falsehood against God will not succeed﴾.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿A brief enjoyment, and for them a painful punishment.﴾

It is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: their benefit in what they are upon of the deeds of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) is a small benefit, and its punishment is great.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 118:

﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you before (this)﴾ — in Surat al-An'am, meaning: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ — the verse. ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by the prohibition ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾. So We forbade them (these things) as a punishment for their disobediences.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 119:

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: they did evil being ignorant, not reflecting on the outcome, because desire had overcome them, and what they intended was the pleasure of their whims, not disobedience to their Master. ﴿Then they repented after that and made amends—indeed your Lord, after it﴾ — after the repentance — ﴿is Forgiving﴾ by covering over the crimes they committed earlier, ﴿Merciful﴾ by confirming the resolutions they made afterward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 120:

﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾ He alone was a nation among the nations, owing to his perfection in all the qualities of goodness, as in the saying:

"It is not far-fetched for God to gather the whole world into one person."

It is also reported from Mujahid: he was a believer alone while all the people were disbelievers. Or, "ummah" here means one who is followed (ma'mum), whom people follow so that they may take goodness from him. ﴿Devoutly obedient to God (qanitan lillah)﴾: he is the one who carries out what God has commanded. Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "Mu'adh was a nation, devoutly obedient to God." It was said to him: "Rather, it is Abraham, peace be upon him." He said: "The ummah is the one who teaches goodness, and the qanit is the one who is obedient to God and His Messenger, and Mu'adh was like that." 

"Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'If Mu'adh were alive, I would have appointed him as my successor, for I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: Abu 'Ubaydah is the trustee of this ummah, and Mu'adh is a nation for God, devoutly obedient to God; between him and God on the Day of Resurrection there is none but the messengers.'"

﴿Upright (hanifan)﴾: inclining away from the religions toward the creed of Islam. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists (mushrikin)﴾: He negated polytheism from him, refuting the Quraysh disbelievers who claimed that they were upon the creed of their father Abraham. The omission of the nun (in "yakun") is for resemblance to the letters of extension (huruf al-lin).

Shākiran li-anʿumihi (grateful for His blessings). It is narrated that he would not eat his midday meal except in the company of a guest. One day he found no guest, so he delayed his meal. Then he saw a group of angels in human form, and he invited them to the food. They appeared to him as though they had leprosy (judhām), and he said: "Now your eating with me has become obligatory." [He said this] in gratitude to God, because He had kept me healthy and tested you.

Ijtabāhu (He chose him): He singled him out and selected him for prophethood. Wa-hadāhu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm (and guided him to a straight path): to the religion of Islam.

﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾: prophethood, wealth, and children; or Allah's exalting of his remembrance, so that every people of religion take him as their leader; or the saying of the one who prays among us, "as You blessed Ibrahim." ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾: among the people of Paradise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 123:

﴿Then We revealed to you: Follow the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham), a man of pure faith (ḥanīfan), and he was not of those who associate partners with God.﴾ In "thumma" (then), there is the magnifying of the rank of our Prophet (ﷺ), the exalting of his station, and the indication that the most noble honour bestowed upon the Friend of God (khalīl Allāh, Ibrahim) is that our Messenger follows his religion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 124:

﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it.﴾ That is: it was made obligatory upon them to venerate it and to refrain from hunting on it. ﴿And indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾ It is narrated that Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, commanded them to set aside one day of the week for worship, and that it should be Friday. But they refused him and said, "We want the day on which Allah finished creating the heavens and the earth," which is Saturday. Only a small group among them agreed to Friday. This was their difference concerning Saturday: some of them chose it, and others chose Friday over it. So Allah permitted them Saturday and tested them by forbidding them to hunt. Those who were content with Friday obeyed the command of Allah, so they did not hunt. But their descendants could not be patient about hunting, so Allah transformed them, but not those others. And He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection, recompensing each of the two groups according to what they deserve.

ادْعُ إلى سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ (ud‘u ila sabili rabbika)

﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ — to Islam — ﴿with wisdom﴾, that is, with the correct and firm statement, which is the clear proof that makes the truth evident and removes doubt; ﴿and good admonition﴾, which is that which leaves them in no doubt that you are advising them with it and intend what benefits them therein; or (p-242) ﴿with the Qur'an﴾, meaning: invite them with the Book, which is wisdom and good admonition. Wisdom (ḥikmah) is knowledge of the ranks of actions, and good admonition (mawʿizah ḥasanah) is that one mixes desire with fear and warning with glad tidings. ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾, that is, by the way which is the best of the ways of argument, with gentleness and softness, without harshness; or by that which awakens hearts, admonishes souls and polishes minds. This is a rebuttal of those who refuse debate in religion. ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ — meaning: He is most knowing of them. So whoever has good in him, a little admonition suffices him, and whoever has no good in him, stratagems fail with him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 126:

﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished.﴾ He called the first act "punishment" (ʿuqūba), and the second is the (true) punishment, because of the parallelism of the speech, as in His saying: "The recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it" (42:40). The second is not an evil deed. The meaning is: if an evil act such as killing or the like is done to you, then respond with its like and do not exceed it. It was narrated that the polytheists mutilated the Muslims on the day of Uhud: they split open their bellies and cut off their private parts. The Prophet ﷺ saw Hamza with his belly split open and said: "By Him in whose name I swear, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place." Then this was revealed, so he expiated for his oath and refrained from what he had intended.

There is no disagreement on the prohibition of mutilation (muthla), since reports prohibiting it have come down, even in the case of the rabid dog. ﴿But if you are patient, it is indeed better for those who are patient.﴾ The pronoun in "lahuwa" (it) refers to the verbal noun (maṣdar) of "ṣabartum" (you are patient), and what is meant by "those who are patient" are the ones addressed; that is, "And if you are patient, your patience is indeed better for you." Placing "those who are patient" in the position of the pronoun is a commendation from God toward them, because they are patient in the face of hardships.

Then He said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿And be patient﴾ — you are the one whom He commanded to resolve upon patience. ﴿And your patience is not except through Allah﴾ — that is, by His enabling (tawfiq) and His steadying (tathbit). ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ — over the disbelievers that they did not believe, and over the believers (p-243) for what the disbelievers did to them, for they have reached their objective. ﴿And do not be in distress because of what they plot﴾. "ḍayq" (distress) is read by Makki, and ḍayq is a lightened form of ḍayyiq (tight), i.e., "in a tight matter." It is also permissible that both are verbal nouns (maṣdar), like al-qīl and al-qawl. The meaning: let your chest not be constricted by their plotting, for it will not be carried out against you.

Indeed, Allah is with those who have taken heed (of Him) and those who are doers of good (ihsan). That is: He is the Protector (waliyy) of those who have avoided evil deeds and the Protector of those who act by acts of obedience. It has been said: whoever is mindful of Allah (ittaqa) in his actions and excels (ahsana) in his deeds, Allah is with him in his states. His being with them (ma'iyyah) means His support in what is commanded and His preservation from what is forbidden.
